title: ALP shift hits 500k on part pension
full_text:
Labor has revealed 500,000 part-rate age pensioners will have to pay more for their private health insurance under its crackdown on rebates for over-65s, as Health Minister Mark Butler considers whether to exempt all pensioners from the changes or only those on the full rate.
Confirmation that half a million part-rate pensioners would be affected, as well as 700,000 full-rate pensioners, comes as the peak body for health funds demanded the Albanese government find “fairer” alternative savings to the $3bn private health insurance rebate cut for over-65s, which Labor wants to use to fund aged care beds and services.
With the Coalition staunchly opposed to the reversal of the Howard-era private health insurance rebate top-ups for older Australians and the Greens calling for an exemption for pensioners, Mr Butler has signalled he’s open to a debate in parliament about carving out full pensioners in a bid to pass his bill through parliament.
Negotiations over the changes, which are due to take effect from April, have been thrown into doubt as the Greens’ health spokesman, Jordon Steele-John, awaits an internal investigation into sexual harassment allegations against him.
It was unclear on Monday who in the Greens would lead talks with the government. The Australian understands any proposal to carve out full pensioners while making part pensioners cop more expensive private health insurance would have to go through the Greens’ partyroom.
Council on the Ageing and National Seniors Australia declared the bill shouldn’t go through regardless of an exemption for all pensioners or full pensioners, warning such a move would be “short-sighted” and a “cheap win”.
“The more people we’ve got taking responsibility and ownership for their own health, which they’ve done for a long period of time, we’ve got to try and keep that running,” NSA chief executive Chris Grice said.
COTA chief executive Patricia Sparrow added: “We’re very concerned about the impact the changes would have on older Australians and our public health system broadly, which is why we’ve been pushing to have the proposal thrown out entirely.” Opposition health and aged care spokeswoman Anne Ruston said the Coalition would support any amendment that carved out full pensioners from the government’s “bad policy” but would still oppose the legislation “because we think it is fundamentally flawed”.
“The (PHI) rebate is already means tested. We wouldn’t stand in the way of pensioners keeping their higher rebate, but a carve-out doesn’t fix this bad policy,” she said.
“When the government announced this policy, it had no idea how many pensioners and part pensioners would be impacted. Without consultation and without modelling, the Albanese Labor government announced a policy that would have seen aged pensioners and our already overburdened public hospitals pay for their budget mismanagement.” The Coalition and the Greens teamed up with crossbenchers last week to discharge the original bill from the notice paper, only for Mr Butler to reintroduce identical legislation to the parliament the next day.
Mr Butler said the government needed to find “responsible” savings to direct new funds into aged care, and his plan returned the private health insurance rebate to its original design to pay households a level of subsidy relevant to their income, not their age.
“We think that’s the right thing to do,” he said. “Australians over 65 will continue to receive the rebate relevant to their income. The government will still pay up to a quarter of people’s private health insurance through the private health insurance rebate.” The government estimates about 1.2 million pensioners have private health insurance and would be affected by the reforms, but was unable to say how much the $3bn save would be reduced if the 700,000 full pensioners were excluded from the overhaul.
The Parliamentary Budget Office estimates 1.5 million older Australians who receive at least a partial pension would be affected, which is 300,000 more people than the government forecasts.
The government’s saving would be halved to $1.56bn if all age pensioners were exempt from the cut to rebate top-up for over-65s, according to the PBO.
Private Healthcare Australia chief executive Rachel David said the government should consider alternatives “that work for taxpayers without putting pensioners and lower-income Australians under greater financial pressure”.
Dr David said Labor could save up to $100m annually by removing the additional price premium paid for medical devices in the private sector compared with public hospitals, arguing the move would cause health insurance premiums to drop and slash the government’s rebate expenditure.
The government could also encourage more higher-income Australians to take out health insurance by increasing the Medicare Levy Surcharge from 1 per cent to 1.5 per cent for singles earning between $105,000 and $123,000 or families earning between $210,000 and $246,000, and lifting it to 3 per cent for higher tiers, Dr David said.
